To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the prison is a vital part, and a potential catalyst, for the resolution of low intensity conflicts.

prisons can play three key roles in the resolution of a low‐intensity intrastate conflict: (1) as part of the post-conflict reconciliation process; (2) as a channel of communication between the state and the insurgent group; and (3) as a bargaining issue in itself.

the role of the prison in low‐intensity internal conflicts is a neglected topic in the literature on conflict resolution and that the prison has three roles in low‐intense conflict resolution: (1) as a part of the post-conflict reconciliation process, (2) as a venue for dialogue, and (3) as a negotiation issue.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: what role do prisons and prisoners play in the process of conflict resolution?
the role of prisons and prisoners in the resolution of intra‐state conflicts and the impact that this can have on the process of post‐conflict reintegration.
the role of the prison as an arena for conflict resolution in low‐intensity internal conflicts.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
prisons and prisoners are a vital part of conflict resolution in low‐intensity intrastate conflicts.
the role of penal policy is important and should be considered as part of any peace‐building process in low‐intensity intrastate conflicts.
the role of the prison is to be a part of the solution rather than a part of the problem.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the prison can be seen as a microcosm of the wider conflict and that the resolution of the conflict is impossible without a resolution of the prison issue.
we can see the prison as a place of punishment and as an instrument of social control, but we also see it as a place for social change and as a place for reconciliation and social inclusion.

the role of penal policy and prisoners in low‐intensity internal conflicts can be divided into three main areas: (a) as part of the post-conflict reconciliation process; (b) as a venue for dialogue and communication between the state and the sub‐state group; and (c) as a negotiation issue in themselves, with release being an important objective for both the state and the group.
The main takeaway from our work is that
prisons are not a marginal part of low‐intensive conflicts, but rather a key component of any conflict resolution strategy.
, despite the lack of literature on the topic and the difficulties of obtaining data, prisons and prisoners can and do play important roles in conflict resolution.
the prison is a crucial part of the conflict resolution process in low‐intensity, intra‐state conflicts.
